{{Short description|Metatheorem}}
In [[metalogic]] and [[metamathematics]], '''Frege's theorem''' is a [[metatheorem]] that states that the [[Peano axiom]]s of [[arithmetic]] can be derived in [[second-order logic]] from [[Hume's principle]]. It was first proven, informally, by [[Gottlob Frege]] in his 1884 ''[[The Foundations of Arithmetic]]''<ref name=:0>[[Gottlob Frege]], ''[[The Foundations of Arithmetic|Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik]]'', Breslau: Verlag von Wilhelm Koebner, 1884, §63.</ref> and proven more formally in his 1893 {{lang|de|Grundgesetze der Arithmetik}} I (''Basic Laws of Arithmetic'' I).<ref name=:1>[[Gottlob Frege]], {{lang|de|Grundgesetze der Arithmetik}} I, Jena: Verlag Hermann Pohle, 1893, §§20 and 47.</ref> The theorem was re-discovered by [[Crispin Wright]] in the early 1980s and has since been the focus of significant work. It is at the core of the [[philosophy of mathematics]] known as [[neo-logicism]] (at least of the [[Scottish School (philosophy of mathematics)|Scottish School]] variety).

== Overview<!--'Basic Law V' redirects here--> ==
In ''[[The Foundations of Arithmetic]]'' (1884), and later, in ''Basic Laws of Arithmetic'' (vol. 1, 1893; vol. 2, 1903), Frege attempted to derive all of the laws of arithmetic from axioms he asserted as logical (see [[logicism]]). Most of these axioms were carried over from his {{lang|de|[[Begriffsschrift]]}}; the one truly new principle was one he called the '''Basic Law V'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--><ref name=:1/> (now known as the [[axiom schema of unrestricted comprehension]]):<ref>Richard Pettigrew, [https://www.mcmp.philosophie.uni-muenchen.de/students/math/basic-set-theory.pdf "Basic set theory"], January 26, 2012, p. 2.</ref> the "value-range" of the function ''f''(''x'') is the same as the "value-range" of the function ''g''(''x'') if and only if ∀''x''[''f''(''x'') = ''g''(''x'')]. However, not only did Basic Law V fail to be a logical proposition, but the resulting system proved to be inconsistent, because it was subject to [[Russell's paradox]].<ref name=Zalta>{{citation|title=[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]|contribution-url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege-theorem/|contribution=Frege's Theorem and Foundations for Arithmetic|first=Edward|last=Zalta|authorlink=Edward Zalta|year=2013}}.</ref>

The inconsistency in Frege's {{lang|de|Grundgesetze}} overshadowed Frege's achievement: according to [[Edward Zalta]], the {{lang|de|Grundgesetze}} "contains all the essential steps of a valid proof (in [[second-order logic]]) of the fundamental propositions of arithmetic from a single consistent principle."<ref name=Zalta/> This achievement has become known as Frege's theorem.<ref name=Zalta/><ref>{{Cite book|title=Logic, Logic, and Logic|url=https://archive.org/details/logiclogiclogic00bool|url-access=limited|last=Boolos|first=George|authorlink=George Boolos|date=1998|publisher=Harvard University Press|others=Edited by Richard C. Jeffrey, introduction by John P. Burgess |isbn=9780674537675|location=Cambridge, Mass|oclc=37509971|page=[https://archive.org/details/logiclogiclogic00bool/page/n161 154]|quote=Frege's startling discovery, of which he may or may not have been fully aware and which has been lost to view since the discovery of Russell's paradox, was that ''arithmetic can be derived in a purely logical system like that of his [[Begriffsschrift]] from this consistent principle and from it alone.''}}</ref>

In [[Propositional calculus|propositional logic]], Frege's theorem refers to this [[tautology (logic)|tautology]]:

:<math>\big(P\to(Q\to R)\big)\to\big((P\to Q)\to(P\to R)\big)</math>

The theorem already holds in one of the weakest logics imaginable, the constructive [[List of Hilbert systems#Implicational propositional calculus|implicational calculus]]. The proof under the [[Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov interpretation]] reads <math>f \mapsto g\mapsto p\mapsto (f(p)\circ g)(p)</math>. 
In words: 
"Let ''f'' denote a reason that ''P'' implies that ''Q'' implies ''R''. And let ''g'' denote a reason that ''P'' implies ''Q''. Then given a ''f'', then given a ''g'', then given a reason ''p'' for ''P'', we know both that ''Q'' holds by ''g'' and that ''Q'' implies ''R'' holds by ''f''. So ''R'' holds."

The [[truth table]] to the right gives a semantic proof. For all possible assignments of ''false'' ({{n&}}) or ''true'' ({{y&}}) to ''P'', ''Q'', and ''R'' (columns 1, 3, 5), each subformula is evaluated according to the rules for [[material conditional]], the result being shown below its main operator. Column 6 shows that the whole formula evaluates to ''true'' in every case, i.e. that it is a tautology. In fact, its [[antecedent (logic)|antecedent]] (column 2) and its [[consequent]] (column 10) are even equivalent.

=== Special cases ===
One commonly takes <math>\neg P</math> to mean <math>P\to\bot</math>, where <math>\bot</math> denotes a false proposition.
With <math>\bot</math> for <math>R</math>, the theorem entails the [[currying|curried]] form of the [[negation introduction]] principle,
:<math>\big((P\to \neg Q\big)\land (P\to Q)\big) \to \neg P</math>
